text: Quantifying “demographic independence” is a vital step in establishing potential conservation units for a species in that it effectively distinguishes migration from within‐population reproduction. This is an important aspect because it allows for an accurate estimate of recruitment. For example, populations may be designated as 'management units' (=MUs) if indeed population growth results from local demography rather than immigration. Of additional interest is the calculation of immigrant ancestry and ascertainment of the temporal context over which immigration occurred. This is because MUs depend largely upon local (self‐sustaining) birth and death rates, and the quantification of ancestry is necessary to validate demographic independence. Dispersal rate is also of immediate interest to conservation biologists, and can be assessed by quantifying genetic divergence among populations. The capacity with which to gauge these benchmarks has now been extended herein to genome‐wide molecular data, in an attempt to adjust an analytical tool that was until now intractable for the next generation sequencing 2. In this study, a popular legacy program for migrant detection (i.e. BayesAss3) has been modified to accept SNP (single nucleotide polymorphism) data. We validated BA3‐SNPs using empirical data to demonstrate its suitability for both high‐performance and desktop computing environments. We also facilitate high analytical throughput by presenting a binary search algorithm that automates MCMC 3. Our BA3‐SNPs‐autotune program required five or fewer rounds of optimization for 99% of input files, with acceptable mixing parameters derived in 100% of our test cases. Runtime for BA3‐SNPs is a function of the number of loci analysed.
Benchmarking yielded an average runtime <32 hr (10 million MCMC generations) 4. The BA3 algorithm remains a viable option for analysing modern SNP datasets.

Accelerated loss of biodiversity is a fundamental issue in the Anthropocene (Lewis & Maslin, 2015), with direct and potentially irreversible consequences for ecosystems at a global scale. To slow this erosion, scientists strive to ascertain at which level biodiversity should be conserved (Douglas & Brunner, 2002). Yet these considerations are complicated both philosophically and methodologically, as they reflect the underlying tension between taxonomy, conservation and the immediacy of adaptive management This dilemma is further compounded by the spatial and temporal scales within which these disciplines are framed. The taxonomy of species, for example, is viewed as a process operating over evolutionary timescales, whereas conservation deals with environmental modifications of a contemporary nature that impact local populations. This gap is effectively bridged by conservation genetics (Allendorf, Hohenlohe, & Luikart, 2010), a multi‐disciplinary science that employs molecular data to delineate units of biodiversity for conservation actions. Such data are often used to distinguish populations and to gauge levels of differentiation at very fine spatial scales (e.g. Hopken, Douglas, & Douglas, 2013; Mussmann et al., 2017). They can also provide a deep historical perspective by deriving genetic patterns that differentiate species (e.g. Douglas, Douglas, Schuett, & Porras, 2006, 2009). Both approaches effectively promote biodiversity management by facilitating the integration of conservation policies at the regional level (Willis & Birks, Recent advances in conservation genomic approaches (Allendorf, 2016) allow for the development of quantitative metrics that can define “conservation units” in non‐model organisms (Holycross & Douglas, 2007; Sullivan et al., 2014). A common approach is the application of RAD (restriction‐site associated DNA) sequencing, where genomic complexity is effectively reduced by employing restriction enzymes to cut genomic DNA at predictable sequence moThis ensures that data remain consistent across individuals, a consideration particularly applicable for organisms that lack an a priori genomic reference (Andrews & Luikart, 2014; Puritz et al., 2014).

Methodological iterations of the original RAD protocol (Baird et al., 2008) have been remarkably prolific with numerous specialized protocols now available (e.g. Peterson, Weber, Kay, Fisher, & Hoekstra, However, genome‐scale data present new computational challenges when placed within a hypothesis‐testing framework. This is magnified by the limited bioinformatics capacity prevailing among conservation practitioners. Both necessitate access to user‐ and computationally friendly algorithms that are powerful enough to parse next generation sequence data yet flexible to accommodate those with limited programming skills. This discrepancy underscores the recognition that development of new molecular methods often outpaces analytical tools. As a result, programs once at the forefront of analysis may become limited in their applicability as molecular One such example is BayesAss (Wilson & Rannala, 2003), a program designed to diagnose demographic independence within and among populations (Palumbi, 2003), a critical step in the establishment of conservation units. Its widespread adoption served to promote the genetic quantification of “management units” in natural populations (Palsbøll, Bérubé, & Allendorf, 2006). A practical example for the utility of this approach is the study of habitat connectivity for organisms of conservation concern; a necessary endeavour to understand and mitigate the negative effects of habitat fragmentation (Holland, Jenkins, & Stevens, 2017; Lean, Hammer, Unmack, Adams, & Beheregaray, 2017; Stevens, Harrisson, Hogan, Cook, & BayesAss remains a popular choice among geneticists despite rapidly increasing dataset sizes. Analytics sourced from the citation indexing service at Web of Science reveal 998 total citations since its publication in 2003, with 346 (34.7%) occurring since January 2016. However, its applicability to large SNP (single nucleotide polymorphisms) datasets has been restricted thus far to relatively small datasets or to those users with access to modified versions of the code (Brauer, Unmack, Smith, Bernatchez, & Beheregaray, 2018; Gonçalves da Silva, Appleyard, & Upston, 2015; Nussberger, Here, we provide new software packages that promote the general application of BayesAss for SNP data. Our modifications to the original program remove the memory limitations that prohibit analysis of RADseq data and modularize the code in order to facilitate future improvements. We also present a new tool that automates The source code for BayesAss version 3.0.4 was downloaded and modified to provide several enhancements that facilitate the analysis of SNP datasets that encompass thousands of loci. This was accomplished by removing the hard‐coded upper limit that constrained the amount of memory allocated for locus storage (N = 420). Instead, we implemented dynamic memory allocation to promote the number of loci processed by BA3‐SNPs, with restrictions manifested only by hardware and operating system limitations. Additional changes (e.g. an object‐oriented programming approach, and streamlining of command line input parsing) also facilitate future extension of the code BA3‐SNPs inherits the functionality of its parent program, including use of the Metropolis–Hastings algorithm for Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling. This algorithm uses a probability distribution to decide if newly proposed values will be accepted or rejected for each MCMC sample. BayesAss implemented this algorithm through user‐specified mixing parameters for migration rates, allele frequencies and inbreeding coefficients. These parameters influence the magnitude of proposed changes. The tuning of these mixing parameters is necessary for efficient MCMC sampling. The original BayesAss documentation instructed users to: (a) manually conduct an exploratory run using the default value of each mixing parameter (i.e. 0.1); (b) evaluate the resulting acceptance rates; and (c) repeat the process by adjusting mixing parameter values for subsequent runs until acceptance rates fall within The above process is impractical when evaluating a large number of input files. We therefore automated the process by employing a binary search algorithm in an additional program, BA3‐SNPs‐autotune. The binary search significantly accelerates the process of tuning the mixing parameters for each unique input by employing automation that eliminates the earlier “guess‐and‐check” process.
The binary search begins with the default mixing parameter value.

If this is deemed too low, a value (i.e. 0.55) halfway between the current and maximum (i.e. 1.0) is then tested. If that value remains low, then logic dictates that all values between 0.1 and 0.55 are eliminated as well. Testing continues by employing values halfway between 0.55 and 1.0. Alternatively, a value midway between 0.1 and 0.55 will be explored if 0.55 is too high. This process continues until either the desired acceptance rates are eventually found for each parameter, or the program reaches a user‐specified maximum number of searches. The original BayesAss manual specifies MCMC acceptance rates between 0.2 and 0.6 as desirable (Gamerman, 1997).

However, BA3‐SNPs‐autotune targets MCMC acceptance rates between 0.35 and 0.45 so as to ensure that final rates fall firmly inside Performance benchmarking was conducted for the above programs by analysing 618 files containing empirical data produced via ddRAD sequencing methods (Peterson et al., 2012). These data were originally used to explore contemporary migration patterns of a small minnow Rhinichthys osculus widely distributed throughout the Colorado River Basin in Western North America (Mussmann, 2018).

Each file contained from 21 to 43 samples (̄x = 30.5, σ = 3.1) genotyped at 632 to 12,408 SNPs (̄x = 8,366.8, σ = 1,918.04). The number of populations (3) was held constant to minimize potential impacts of BA3‐SNPs‐autotune was first used to find optimal mixing parameters for each run, with exploratory analyses employing 10,000 MCMC generations. A maximum of 10 exploratory analyses were conducted for each dataset. The number of repetitions required to find optimal mixing parameters was recorded for each, and mixing parameters verified to produce adequate MCMC acceptance rates The final mixing parameters were applied to each dataset in BA3‐ SNPs. Ten million Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) generations were calculated for each run. The time needed to analyze each file was recorded. Linear models were evaluated to explain the runtime as a function of the number of samples, the number of loci, and the number of samples and loci (R Development Core Team, 2018). All tests were performed on a computer equipped with dual Intel Xeon E5‐4627 3.30GHz processors, 265GB RAM, and with a 64‐bit Linux environment. A single processor core was used per analysis.

To find optimal mixing parameters, BA3‐SNPs‐autotune required between three and 10 rounds of optimization per data file (̄x = 4.15, σ = 0.72) (Figure 1). The four that required 10 rounds of optimization were deemed statistical outliers. BA3‐SNPs runs associated with these four files ultimately had acceptance rates for each parameter that fell within the recommended values specified in the original BayesAss user manual, despite requiring ten rounds of BA3‐SNPs completed the analysis of all files in 1.91 to 93.51 hr (̄x = 31.11, σ = 11.85). Computational speed was assessed relative to the number of individuals per data file (Figure 2a), and the number of loci (Figure 2b). A weak yet significant correlation was found between sample size and run time (R2 = 0.015, p = 0.00134). However, it appears the number of loci evaluated is a more accurate predictor of runtime (R2 = 0.307, p < 2.2 × 10−16). Modest gains in model fit were achieved by couching runtime as a function of both samples and loci (R2 = 0.3346, p < 2.2 × 10−16). Migration rates calculated by BA3‐SNPs were largely as expected, with samples from geographically proximate sites along linear, free‐flowing freshwater streams exhibiting elevated rates of migration (Mussmann, 2018).

The enhancements to BayesAss that promote the analysis of contemporary SNP data represent necessary upgrades to a valuable algorithm. Our preliminary testing verified that these parameters could be identified using low numbers of MCMC generations per exploratory run.

The program rarely required more than 5 rounds of optimization to obtain suitable parameters. This, in turn, will greatly aid researchers We stress that utilization of BA3‐SNPs‐autotune is solely for the purpose of tuning mixing parameters, and is not a replacement for responsible use of MCMC‐based algorithms. Users should verify that mixing parameters selected for BA3‐SNPs remain within the acceptable range after conducting longer runs of the program. Users should also read the original BayesAss user manual, especially sections that discuss the tuning of mixing parameters. We encourage users to explore this process manually via the original documentation as an exercise in understanding the underlying process autoUsers must still assess mixing, convergence and effective sample size as they would with any Bayesian software when conducting their final runs of BA3‐SNPs for data collection. The trace file output by BA3‐SNPs remains unchanged in format from the original version, meaning it is readable by the Tracer software package (Rambaut, Drummond, Xie, Baele, & Suchard, 2018). Users are encouraged to make their MCMC trace files available as supplemental information, One important benefit of BayesAss3 was its capacity to designate populations as 'management units' or MUs (defined as demographically independent populations whose growth depends largely on local birth/death rates rather than those accrued from immigration: Palsbøll et al., 2006). Of additional interest is the capacity not only to identify immigrants but also to quantify their contributions to population expansion. The dichotomy is important. MUs depend largely upon local (self‐sustaining) birth and death rates, and it is essential to effectively bookmark their demographic independence (Waples & Gaggiotti, 2006). By the same token, dispersal rate is of immediate interest to conservation biologists because it reflects population connectivity, and its impact on genetic divergence can now be gauged among populations. BA3‐SNPs has now extended the capacity to assay these population parameters by employing SNPs as a data source.

Our study is thus a validation that key legacy programs, once suitably modified, can still maintain their functionality in a more contemporary and data‐heavy environment. Although innovation is always important, legacy programs have been thoroughly vetted through years of application to biological problems. BayesAss is no exception, with previous studies identifying specific applications that may be problematic for researchers (Faubet, Waples, & Gaggiotti, 2007;
We encourage all users of BA3‐SNPs to consider the implications of these papers in their experimental design.

Legacy software is frequently considered obsolete as molecular methods evolve, such that developers opt to “reinvent the wheel” rather than update existing software (Altschul et al., 2013). This defeats an often‐cited benefit of open‐source software (Prlić & Procter, 2012). The software packages described herein not only to modernize migration analyses to accommodate next‐generation sequence data, but also to increase their accessibility to a broad range of conservation geneticists and genomicists. This availability is vital to both the widespread application of existing methods and the promotion of their community‐sourced improvements (Howison & Bullard, 2016).
